text.p: Monica Seles is determined to rise above hurtful public criticism of her appearance and seize the opportunity to add a Wimbledon singles title to her grand slam collection.
The departure of Conchita Martinez on Sunday, together with Steffi Graf's injury absence, has ensured there will be a new women's champion this year and Seles remains a prominent contender.
But her current visit to London has been overshadowed by her father's continuing battle against cancer and the publication of a series of unflattering photographs taken during her recent matches.

The most recent appeared on Sunday morning beneath the less-than-polite headline "Wobbledon", yet Seles insists she is less bothered than she was five years ago during the infamous 'gruntometer' championships of 1992.
"I just think sometimes it's not fair, but I guess it comes with the territory," said Seles, after finally shaking off the second round challenge of American Kristina Brandi 5-7 6-3 6-3.
"They're obsessed about something all the time. In 1992 it bugged me a lot, but after that I learned a lot. This year it doesn't matter.
"To me it's particularly hurtful when they put words in my mouth. When I read the article, I'm like 'No, I didn't say that', but my Dad taught me to take it all in good spirits."
Karolj Seles is monitoring his daughter's progress on television but has been advised not to get too involved in her matches.
"A few people have told him it might be better if he doesn't watch it live. He just tapes it and my mum and I will call him and tell him the score."
Even Seles, though, concedes that her form and fitness are nowhere near what they were before her stabbing in Hamburg in April 1993.

There were times, even against the 87th-ranked Brandi, when her lack of mobility was cruelly exposed and it was not until the last few games of the final set that her victory could be described as comfortable.
"There are so many things," admitted Seles, when pressed to compare her current state with the younger version who picked up eight grand slam titles in less than three years.
"After two and a half years of not picking up a racket, my timing is not the same and I've never really had the chance to practise a lot and get back the consistency that I had before."
"This year, in terms of tournaments, I haven't played that much but after the French Open I was ranked number two so it's not as bad as sometimes I make it out to be.
"But, for me, what's been the most disappointing is not doing well in the Grand Slams. To get back to the top is going to take a lot of things."
